questions.question: Which directory conventionally holds system log files?
questions.explanation: /var holds variable data that changes at runtime; logs live in /var/log. /etc is for configuration, /usr for installed software, /opt for optional third-party packages.

questions.question: What does `chmod 640 report.txt` grant?
options: Owner rwx, group r, others none
Owner rw, group r, others none
Owner rw, group w, others r
Owner r, group rw, others none
questions.explanation: Octal digits map to owner/group/others: 6 = 4+2 = rw-, 4 = r--, 0 = ---. So the owner can read/write, the group can read, and others have no access.

questions.question: Which command shows free disk space per filesystem in human-readable units?
questions.explanation: df (disk free) reports per-filesystem usage; -h makes it human-readable. du measures directory usage, free shows memory, ls lists files.

questions.question: What is the difference between `kill -15` and `kill -9`?
options: -15 sends SIGTERM (graceful, catchable); -9 sends SIGKILL (immediate, uncatchable)
They are aliases for the same signal
questions.explanation: SIGTERM (15) asks the process to shut down and lets it run cleanup handlers. SIGKILL (9) is enforced by the kernel and cannot be caught — the process gets no chance to clean up, so it's a last resort.

questions.question: What does `command > out.log 2>&1` do?
options: Sends stdout to out.log and discards stderr
Sends stderr to out.log and stdout to the terminal
Sends both stdout and stderr to out.log
questions.explanation: `>` redirects stdout (fd 1) to the file; `2>&1` then redirects stderr (fd 2) to wherever fd 1 currently points — the file. Order matters: `2>&1 > out.log` would leave stderr on the terminal.

questions.question: In a bash script, what does `set -euo pipefail` do?
options: Exits on errors, errors on unset variables, and fails a pipeline if any command in it fails
Runs the script in a restricted shell
questions.explanation: -e exits on any command failure, -u treats unset variables as errors, and pipefail makes a pipeline's exit status the first failure instead of the last command's status. Together they make scripts fail fast and loudly.

questions.question: `tail -f app.log` prints the last lines of the file and then keeps printing new lines as they are appended.
questions.explanation: True. -f means 'follow' — tail stays attached and streams new lines, which is the standard way to watch a live log.

questions.question: Deleting a large file always frees its disk space immediately, even if a process still has the file open.
questions.explanation: False. If a process holds the file open, the inode stays allocated until the file descriptor closes — df won't drop. That's why truncating (`> app.log`) is often better than deleting a live log, and why `lsof +L1` finds deleted-but-open files.

questions.question: A deploy fails with 'Permission denied' writing to /opt/app/releases. `ls -ld /opt/app/releases` shows `drwxr-xr-x root root`. The deploy runs as user `deploy`. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Run the whole deploy as root
questions.explanation: Give ownership to the user that needs to write. Running deploys as root violates least privilege, and 777 lets every user on the system write there — both are common but dangerous shortcuts.

questions.question: An app reports 'address already in use' on port 8080 at startup. Which command best identifies the conflicting process?
questions.explanation: ss shows sockets with the owning process (-p), listening only (-l), TCP/UDP (-t/-u), numeric ports (-n). `ps | grep 8080` only matches '8080' in command lines, which is unreliable — the port number usually isn't in the process name.

questions.question: Write the command to recursively search for the string ERROR in /var/log/app, showing line numbers.
questions.explanation: grep -r recurses into directories, -n prefixes each match with its line number. Order of combined flags doesn't matter.

questions.question: Write the command to restart the nginx service using systemd (without sudo).
questions.explanation: systemctl <verb> <unit> is the systemd pattern. `restart` stops then starts; `reload` re-reads config without dropping connections when the service supports it.

questions.question: Which command shows the last 50 log lines for the systemd unit `api` and keeps following?
questions.explanation: journalctl reads the systemd journal: -u filters by unit, -n limits history, -f follows. `systemctl logs` doesn't exist; the unit may not write to a file in /var/log at all.

questions.question: Environment variables set with `export VAR=value` in one shell session are automatically visible in all other already-running sessions.
questions.explanation: False. Exported variables propagate only to child processes started afterwards from that shell. Other sessions never see them — which is why service env vars belong in systemd unit files or /etc/environment.
